Short answer: It depends: Jane Doe may be able to deduct her home office expenses if she meets the specific requirements, but the sources indicate that employees generally cannot deduct these expenses [IRS Pub 334 (2025), p. 41], [IRS Pub 587 (2025), p. 3].

To deduct expenses related to the part of a home used for business, specific requirements must be met [IRS Pub 334 (2025), p. 41]. The home office must qualify as the principal place of business or meet clients, patients, or customers there regularly and substantially [IRS Pub 587 (2025), p. 3]. If the home office is not used exclusively for business, the employee cannot claim a deduction for its use [IRS Pub 334 (2025), p. 41]. The client's notes state that all home office expenses are fully deductible for employees, citing 26 U.S.C. § 280A, but this legal statement is not supported by the sources provided [client-upload.pdf, p. 1]. Short answer: It depends: meals may be deductible if they meet specific criteria [26 U.S.C. § 274(k)-(l)], [26 U.S.C. § 274(n)(1)], [26 CFR 1.274-12(a)(4)].

No deduction shall be allowed for the expense of any food or beverages unless the expense is not lavish or extravagant under the circumstances and the taxpayer (or an employee of the taxpayer) is present at the furnishing of such food or beverages [26 U.S.C. § 274(k)-(l)]. Only 50 percent of meal expenses is allowed as a deduction [26 U.S.C. § 274(n)(1)]. Food or beverage expenses paid or incurred while traveling away from home in pursuit of a trade or business are subject to deduction limitations and substantiation requirements [26 CFR 1.274-12(a)(4)].
